content: Training curricula for the care of small and sick newborns should be updated promptly and efficiently, in collaboration with professional bodies. In-service training and supervisory courses must be tailored to the professional requirements of health workers, taking into account the content, duration, and selection procedures for participants. These courses should also address staff turnover, particularly in resource-limited settings. Standardized tools for supervision should be developed to enable supervisors to support health workers in delivering integrated and comprehensive care for small and sick newborns. Strategies to optimize the use of human resources should be implemented. Job aids or tools for use at various levels of healthcare facilities and within communities must be developed or updated to include all essential information. Supply chain management strategies should be improved based on local needs. This includes creating protocols for obtaining and maintaining stock, encouraging health workers to monitor stock levels, and strengthening coordination and follow-up for medicines and healthcare supplies. National guidelines and facility-based protocols should be developed or revised to align with these recommendations. Effective supervision, communication, and transport links between community, primary, and higher-level facilities must be established to ensure efficient referral pathways. Successful implementation strategies should be documented and shared as best practices. Community sensitization activities should disseminate information about the importance of care components and the rights of infants to receive appropriate care for their health and well-being. In humanitarian emergencies, recommendations should be adapted to align with other response strategies, considering the unique needs, values, and preferences of families and infants. Context-specific tools may be required in addition to standard tools to support implementation in these settings. Barriers to effective implementation and scale-up of these recommendations may arise from the behaviors of families or health workers, as well as the organization of care or service delivery. A phased approach to adoption, adaptation, and implementation may help address these challenges. Strategies to overcome these barriers are detailed in each chapter of the guideline. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) has identified critical knowledge gaps that require primary research. Research questions were prioritized based on their potential to improve care and outcomes for preterm or low-birth-weight infants, their public health impact, feasibility, and ability to inform new or revised recommendations. These include questions on growth, neurodevelopment, breastfeeding, probiotics, emollients, and respiratory support, among others. The dissemination of recommendations will occur through WHO regional and country offices, ministries of health, professional associations, collaborating centers, and other partners. Recommendations will be available on the WHO website, in print, and in multiple languages. Technical meetings and evidence briefs will be developed to share recommendations and address context-specific issues. Monitoring and evaluation of the recommendations' implementation and impact will occur at health service, subnational, and national levels. Indicators such as neonatal mortality, early breastfeeding, postnatal care, and kangaroo mother care will be tracked. A full monitoring framework will be developed, and indicators will be reviewed and updated as needed. The guideline will follow a living guidelines approach, with regular updates based on new evidence. A Guideline Steering Group will prioritize questions for recommendation development and updating. Recommendations supported by low-certainty evidence will be reviewed, and updates will be made when new evidence emerges. If no new evidence is identified, recommendations will be revalidated.
